faqs.q: Do I really need to care about Bing and Ecosia in Germany?

faqs.a: It is the legally required publisher information every commercial German website must display: company name, address, contact details, registration numbers and the responsible person. It comes from section 5 of the DDG, and it affects SEO indirectly but seriously. A missing or incomplete Impressum can trigger an Abmahnung, a formal warning letter that routinely costs four figures, and German users distrust sites without one, which hurts conversions. Every audit I do in Germany checks the Impressum first, because it is both a legal requirement and a trust signal.
faqs.q: What is an Impressum, and does it affect my SEO?

faqs.a: It depends on your audience, and getting it wrong costs conversions. The formal Sie is the default for B2B, professional services, finance, healthcare and anyone selling to an older or traditional audience. The informal du works for startups, youth brands, outdoor and lifestyle. Mixing them, or switching mid-site, reads as careless to German readers. For SEO the choice also shapes keyword targeting, because search queries themselves use one form or the other. I decide this in the audit based on your customers, then keep it consistent across every page.
faqs.q: Should my German website use Sie or du?

Sites that get this right earn trust; sites with dark patterns get reported. h1: SEO Expert in Germany for Mittelstand Businesses That Want Measurable Growth
intro:
Germany is the biggest search market in the EU, and it plays by rules that outsiders consistently underestimate. About 84 million people, the continent's largest economy, and a business landscape dominated by the Mittelstand: family-run small and medium enterprises that think in decades, decide carefully and reward suppliers who prove themselves. German is the language of search here, and German customers are research-heavy buyers. They compare, they read the detailed reviews, they check the test reports, and they decide based on evidence rather than advertising claims. A ranking without substance behind it does not convert in Germany. A ranking with substance behind it converts better than almost anywhere.

Search in Germany is less of a Google monopoly than in most of Europe. Google holds around 80%, but Bing has a genuine 10% share, driven by Windows defaults on the office PCs where B2B research happens, and Ecosia, the Berlin-based privacy search engine, posts its best home-market numbers anywhere. DuckDuckGo and Yahoo split the rest. That fragmentation is a strategic fact: a Germany-only SEO plan that ignores Bing and Ecosia leaves a meaningful slice of commercial searches on the table, particularly in B2B. I optimize for all of them, because the German market rewards whoever shows up everywhere the customer looks.

The business hubs each have their own character. Berlin is the startup capital, Munich pairs tech with automotive and engineering, Hamburg runs on media and logistics, Frankfurt is finance, the Rhine-Ruhr region around Cologne and Dusseldorf is industrial density, Stuttgart is automotive engineering. Keyword competition, search behavior and even the formality of the language differ between them. A Munich engineering firm and a Berlin SaaS startup need different keyword strategies, different content depth and different review platforms, and a national generic campaign serves neither properly.

Then there is the legal and cultural layer that makes Germany unique. Every commercial website needs an Impressum under section 5 of the DDG, and a missing one can trigger an Abmahnung, a formal warning letter that routinely costs four figures. Cookie consent runs under section 25 TDDDG with DSK guidance demanding real button parity between accept and refuse. The Hamburg authority's 35.3 million euro fine against H&M showed that enforcement has teeth. German users notice these things: a compliant, transparent site earns trust, and trust is what German customers buy. My SEO work in Germany is built for this reality. Proper German copy with the right Sie or du, Bing and Ecosia included, citations across Das Ortliche and Gelbe Seiten, reviews on the platforms Germans check, and technical audits that treat legal compliance as a ranking and conversion factor. Methodical work for a methodical market.

section1.body:
Germany's citation landscape is built on legacy directory brands that successfully moved online. Das Ortliche (dasoertliche.de) and Gelbe Seiten (gelbeseiten.de) are the former phone-book giants, and Google still reads them as authoritative corroboration that your business exists. Alongside them sit GoYellow, meinestadt.de, which also carries real local traffic, and the international aggregators. For B2B, Wer liefert was (wlw.de) is the industrial sourcing directory where German buyers actually look for suppliers. A German citation footprint that skips these domestic sources looks thin to both Google and the customer.

My audits start with NAP consistency done the German way. Company names must match the Handelsregister entry, including legal forms like GmbH or UG, because German business identity is formal and Google cross-references it. Addresses follow German conventions exactly, street, house number, postal code, and umlauts must survive intact through every data feed: when Muller becomes Muller or Strabe becomes Strasse inconsistently, Google sees different businesses. I check Das Ortliche, Gelbe Seiten, GoYellow, meinestadt.de and the aggregators for every variation, merge duplicates, close listings for old locations and configure service-area businesses for the regions they serve without fake storefront addresses.

Review platforms are part of the citation footprint in Germany in a way they are not elsewhere. ProvenExpert for services, Jameda for medical practices, Kununu for employer reputation: these profiles rank, they get read, and they feed the trust evaluation German customers perform before calling. I make sure your business is claimed, correct and consistent on the platforms that matter for your trade, with descriptions in proper German. Then we maintain everything. New locations, changed hours, new services, every update goes out consistently across the footprint. In Germany's evidence-driven market, a messy citation footprint does not just cost rankings. It contradicts the precision your customers expect from a German business, and that contradiction costs the sale.

section2.body:
The Google Business Profile in Germany punches above its weight, because German customers use it as a research tool, not just a phone book. It sits above organic results with your reviews, hours, photos and call button, and for local searches it is often the entire comparison interface. A German searching for a Steuerberater in Munich or a Handwerker in Hamburg will open the three map pack profiles, read the reviews in detail and call one. German reviewers write thorough, specific reviews, which makes a well-reviewed profile an enormously persuasive asset. An incomplete or review-poor profile does not just lose the ranking. It loses the comparison that follows.

I rebuild German profiles for how Germans evaluate them. Categories chosen for the German terms with real search volume, not translated approximations. A business description in proper German, with the right Sie or du for your audience, spelling out services and service areas the way customers type them. Photos are essential: real images of premises, team and work, because German customers are skeptical of businesses they cannot see. Opening hours exact, including holiday variations, and special hours posted in advance. Attributes filled in completely, from wheelchair accessibility to appointment requirements, because Germans filter on details.

Reviews are where German profiles are won. I install a review process that asks in German at the right moment, with a direct link removing every friction point, and I prepare reply templates so every review gets a professional response. German customers notice unanswered reviews, and they notice defensive replies even more. A profile with thirty detailed German reviews and thoughtful owner responses will beat a competitor with a better website and five reviews, consistently. Then we keep the profile working: regular posts, prompt answers to questions, current products and services. Google rewards maintained profiles, and in Germany, where the customer researches before calling, a living profile is the most credible salesperson you have. It works around the clock, in the language your customers trust, and almost none of your competitors maintain theirs.

why.body:
Germany needs specialized SEO because generic approaches collide with German specifics at every level. The first collision is language. German compounds create keywords that do not exist in English: the search term is often a single long compound word, and getting the compound wrong means targeting a phrase nobody types. Keyword research has to start from German compounds, German search behavior and the formal-informal split between Sie and du, which shapes both copy and queries. Translated English keyword lists produce the wrong compounds, the wrong formality and the wrong intent. I have seen international businesses run German SEO for years on translated lists and wonder why conversions never came. The language was the problem from day one.

The second collision is the search landscape itself. Germany is one of the few European markets where Bing matters: a genuine 10% share, concentrated on the office desktops where B2B buying research happens, plus Ecosia's unusually strong home-market position driven by German privacy and sustainability values. A Google-only strategy abandons a real share of commercial intent, especially in B2B. Specialized German SEO optimizes for Bing Webmaster guidelines and Ecosia's preferences alongside Google, tracks rankings across engines and builds content that earns links from the German-language web, which is what moves all three.

The third collision is legal and cultural. The Impressum requirement, the Abmahnung risk, the TDDDG consent rules with DSK button-parity guidance, the 35.3 million euro H&M fine: Germany enforces its digital rules, and German customers have internalized them. A site with a missing Impressum, a manipulative cookie banner or sloppy data practices feels untrustworthy to Germans before they read a word of content. My audits treat legal compliance as an SEO factor, because in Germany it is one: trust signals convert, and compliance is the foundation of trust. Generic SEO treats Germany as a big English market with umlauts. Specialized SEO treats it as what it is: Europe's largest, most methodical, most regulation-aware search market, where precision wins.
